nodes.title: Business
nodes.heading: Item 1. Business
nodes.start_phrase: Microsoft is a technology company whose mission is to empower every person and every organization on the planet to achieve more.
nodes.summary:
- Forward-Looking Statements: Cautionary note about estimates and projections, references to risk and MD&A sections, and no obligation to update.
- Company Overview and Strategy: Microsoft’s mission to empower people and organizations; “mobile-first, cloud-first” strategy; broad portfolio across software, services, devices, and online advertising operating in 190+ countries.
- Strategic Ambitions:
  - Reinvent productivity and business processes via Office 365, Dynamics, and cross-platform, intelligent, collaborative solutions.
  - Build the intelligent cloud platform with Azure and server products (SQL Server, Windows Server, Visual Studio, System Center), emphasizing hybrid cloud, security, identity, data/analytics, and developer services.
  - Create more personal computing centered on Windows 10 as a service, new input methods (speech, pen, gesture, AR), OEM ecosystem, first-party devices, and monetization through services, gaming, and search.
- Future Focus Areas: Productivity and collaboration, cloud services, Windows platform across devices and cloud, innovative devices, and machine learning to make technology more intuitive.
- Operating Segments (reorganized FY2016):
  - Productivity and Business Processes: Office Commercial (incl. Office 365, Exchange, SharePoint, Skype for Business, CALs), Office Consumer (incl. Office 365 consumer, Skype, Outlook.com, OneDrive), Dynamics (ERP/CRM).
  - Intelligent Cloud: Server products and cloud services (incl. Azure) and Enterprise Services (Premier Support, Consulting).
  - More Personal Computing: Windows (OEM/volume licensing, embedded, patent licensing, MSN display ads, Windows Phone licensing), Devices (Surface, phones, accessories; phone business restructuring and feature phone divestiture), Gaming (Xbox hardware, Xbox Live, first/third-party content; Minecraft acquisition; Xbox One S), Search advertising (Bing, partnerships incl. Yahoo!).
- Key Revenue Drivers:
  - Shift to Office 365 and cloud subscriptions; CALs and volume licensing for commercial customers.
  - Windows OEM license volumes and mix, market/geography dynamics, channel inventory, pricing, and piracy; Windows volume licensing more tied to information worker counts.
  - Azure scale and higher-level services; enterprise support and consulting engagements.
- Competition:
  - Productivity/Dynamics vs. Adobe, Apple, Cisco, Google, IBM, Oracle, SAP, Salesforce, Infor, Sage, NetSuite, and numerous web/mobile app providers.
  - Intelligent Cloud vs. Linux/Red Hat, IBM/Oracle/Java ecosystem, open-source stacks (Apache, MySQL, PHP), VMware, Amazon, Google, Salesforce; advantages include hybrid cloud and scale.
  - More Personal Computing vs. Apple and Google for OS/devices; Sony and Nintendo for consoles; EA and Activision for games; Amazon/Apple/Google for marketplaces; Google and social platforms for ads.
- Operations: Global operations centers (US, Ireland, Singapore, etc.), worldwide datacenters, product localization; manufacturing of phones (primarily Vietnam) with feature phone business sale; other devices made by third-party manufacturers.
- Research & Development and IP:
  - R&D spend ~$12B annually (FY2016/2015), engineering groups for Apps & Services, Cloud & Enterprise, Windows & Devices.
  - Strong IP portfolio (61,000+ issued patents; 35,000+ pending), active licensing and cross-licensing, Microsoft Research collaborations worldwide.
- Distribution, Sales, and Marketing:
  - Channels include OEMs (Direct OEMs and system builders), distributors/resellers (LSPs, VARs), online, and Microsoft retail stores.
  - Named partners include Acer, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Samsung, Ingram Micro, Tech Data, CDW, Insight, SHI; Dynamics via specialized channel partners.
  - Online delivery of services (Office 365, Azure, Dynamics CRM Online, Bing/MSN, Xbox Live, Outlook.com, OneDrive, Windows Store) with programs for SMBs and operator channels.
- Licensing Programs:
  - Enterprise Agreement (perpetual or subscription with Software Assurance), MPSA (consolidated purchasing), Select Plus retirement/migration to MPSA, Open programs (Open License/Open Value), and Microsoft Online Subscription Agreement.
  - Partner programs: Cloud Solution Provider, Services Provider License Agreement, Online Services Reseller, ISV Royalty.
- Customers: Broad base across consumers, SMBs, enterprises, public sector, ISPs, developers, and OEMs; no single customer >10% of revenue; minimal backlog.
- Executive Leadership: Listing of key executives (CEO Satya Nadella; CMO Chris Capossela; EVP Global Sales/Marketing/Operations Jean-Philippe Courtois; EVP HR Kathleen Hogan; CFO Amy Hood; EVP Business Development Margaret Johnson; President/Chief Legal Officer Brad Smith) with brief role histories (partially provided).

nodes.title: Risk Factors
nodes.heading: Item 1A. Risk Factors
nodes.start_phrase:
Our operati ons and financial results are subject to various risks and uncertainties, includi ng those described below , that could adversely affect our
business, financial condition, results of operations, cash flows, and the trading price of our common stock.
nodes.summary:
- Overview/Investor communications: Points readers to Microsoft’s Investor Relations website for corporate governance documents (articles, bylaws, governance guidelines, committee charters, codes of conduct/ethics), CSR policies, news/announcements, and options for email/RSS alerts; notes that website content isn’t part of SEC filings; acknowledges use of social media for potentially material disclosures and directs investors to listed channels.

- Item 1A – Risk Factors:
  - Competition: Intense competition across platforms, ecosystems, and devices; challenges from vertically integrated rivals; pressure on Windows PC licensing from mobile/tablet platforms and low/no-cost operating systems; dependence on attracting developers versus competing app stores; potential margin compression.
  - Business models: Tension between proprietary license model and competitors’ ad-supported/free and open-source approaches; open-source and ad-funded rivals can undercut prices and shift customer expectations, pressuring revenue and margins.
  - Cloud/mobile transition: Strategic pivot to “mobile-first, cloud-first” brings execution risks, evolving pricing/delivery models, high infrastructure and R&D costs that may lower margins; need for reliability, security, cross-platform availability, and third-party developer engagement; uncertainty over user adoption and monetization.
  - Investments/innovation: Large, ongoing investments in Windows, Office, Bing, Azure, Office 365, Xbox, devices (Surface, phones, tablets, PCs); risk that offerings don’t deliver expected functionality, adoption, or profitability; potential delays/defects in new technologies.
  - Windows 10: Free upgrades, scale and complexity risks; potential negative user or regulatory reactions (including privacy/data practices), litigation, and failure to realize post-license monetization.
  - M&A/Alliances: Integration, strategy fit, distraction, and ROI risks, highlighted by the LinkedIn acquisition; potential for delayed/smaller-than-expected benefits.
  - Goodwill/intangibles: Risk of impairment charges if acquisitions underperform; cites past impairments in the phone business and increased balances from LinkedIn.
  - Intellectual property: Difficulty policing piracy globally; potential declines in patent royalty income due to legal changes, disputes, or technology/pricing shifts; exposure to third-party IP claims leading to damages, injunctions, redesigns, or costly licenses; risk from unauthorized source code disclosure.
  - Cybersecurity and privacy: Evolving threats to internal IT and customer-facing products/services, including cloud; potential outages, theft of IP, reputational harm, and increased security costs; liability and reputational risk from personal data breaches; government data requests and cross-border data handling concerns may affect adoption and costs.
  - Service reliability/operations: Risks of outages, data loss, or insufficient capacity across expanding online services and third-party hosting platforms (Azure, Office 365, Xbox Live, etc.); potential contractual liability and reputational damage.
  - Competition law/regulation: Global antitrust scrutiny (EU, U.S., China) may constrain product design, interoperability, licensing terms, and Windows 10 monetization; coopetition with OEMs heightens compliance risk; potential fines, product changes, or market withdrawals.
  - Anti-corruption/trade: Exposure to FCPA and similar laws; inquiries and compliance risks; potential sanctions, penalties, reputational harm; evolving telecom, privacy, and content regulations may increase costs or limit offerings.
  - Data protection/cross-border transfers: Post–EU Safe Harbor invalidation creates uncertainty for EU–U.S. data flows; potential for fragmented or burdensome rules increasing costs and compliance risk.
  - Talent: Competition for skilled employees, immigration limits, and succession planning risks; employment law changes could raise costs.
  - Litigation: Broad exposure to claims tied to products (e.g., Windows 10), transactions, and employment; adverse outcomes could be material.
  - Tax: Uncertain outcomes of global audits and potential legislative changes affecting foreign earnings and repatriation; possible material impacts on tax expense and cash flows.
  - Product quality/supply chain: Hardware (Xbox, Surface, phones) and software defects, reliance on sole-source components, supply constraints, inventory risk, and assembly concentration in Asia; growing accessibility requirements pose compliance/revenue risks.
  - Global/economic risks: Operational challenges in emerging markets, FX volatility, catastrophic events, geopolitical instability, climate/energy impacts; macro weakness or government budget limits (including U.S. federal spending) may reduce IT demand; channel partner financial stress; customer credit risk; investment portfolio exposure to market/sovereign credit events.

- Item 1B – Unresolved Staff Comments: None from SEC staff outstanding as of fiscal year-end 2016.

- Item 2 – Properties: Headquarters in Redmond, WA; approximately 15 million square feet in King County (about 10 million owned on ~500 acres, ~5 million leased) plus additional U.S. office/retail/datacenter space; owned international sites include R&D in China/India, operations in Ireland/Singapore, phone manufacturing (primarily Vietnam), and U.K. facilities; major leased offices in Finland, China, India, Germany, U.K., Canada, Japan; total global footprint ~45.9 million square feet (U.S.: 26.1; International: 19.8; Owned: 25.4; Leased: 20.5).

- Key risk factor: Adverse economic/market conditions
  - Inflation, recession, or weaker economic conditions could lower IT spending; declines in demand for PCs/servers and other devices would reduce revenue.
  - Heavy exposure to U.S. government contracts; shutdowns, debt ceiling issues, or budget constraints could limit or delay federal IT spending.
  - Dependence on an extensive partner/retail network and OEMs for product distribution; bankruptcies or disruptions among partners could impair sales channels.
  - Customer financial stress could raise allowances for doubtful accounts and receivable write-offs.
  - Investment portfolio risks (credit, liquidity, market, interest rate), with significant U.S. government securities; prolonged market declines or a U.S. credit downgrade could cause impairments and hurt financial results.

- Properties overview

  - International owned/leased facilities: R&D in China and India; operations in Ireland and Singapore; phone manufacturing mainly in Vietnam; facilities in the U.K. Largest leased offices: Finland, China, India, Germany, U.K., Canada, Japan.

nodes.summary:
- Document type and scope: Part II of Microsoft’s Form 10-K, primarily Item 7 (Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations) with related segment results, operating expenses, tax, liquidity, and market risk disclosures; includes notes on key adjustments and deferrals impacting results.

- Key accounting impacts and footnotes:
  - Windows 10 net revenue deferral of $6.6B decreased FY2016 operating income, net income, and diluted EPS by $6.6B, $4.6B, and $0.58.
  - FY2016 phone-related charges: $630M asset impairments and $480M restructuring (total $1.1B; EPS impact $0.11).
  - FY2015 phone-related charges: $7.5B goodwill/asset impairments and $2.5B integration/restructuring (total $10.0B; EPS impact $1.15).
  - Adoption of new deferred tax balance sheet classification in FY2016.
  - Earlier notable items include EC fine (2013), Surface RT inventory adjustment (2013), and goodwill impairment in the former Online Services Division (2012).

- Strategy and FY2016 highlights:
  - Focus on three ambitions: productivity and business processes, intelligent cloud, more personal computing.
  - Commercial cloud annualized revenue run rate >$12.1B; Azure revenue up 113% with major usage growth.
  - Office 365 Consumer subscribers 23.1M; Dynamics CRM Online seat additions more than doubled.
  - Windows 10 active on 350M+ devices.
  - Xbox Live monthly active users up 33% to 49M.

- Major transactions and restructuring:
  - Agreement to acquire LinkedIn for $26.2B, to be financed primarily with new debt (expected close in calendar 2016).
  - Announced sale of entry-level feature phone business for $350M (expected close 2H 2016).
  - Ongoing restructuring and strategic refocus of smartphone hardware; anticipated continued decline in phone units and expenses.

- Industry trends and risks:
  - Highly dynamic, competitive market with evolving devices, cloud services, and business models; need to attract/retain talent; FX headwinds.
  - Seasonality: Q2 typically strongest.

nodes.title: ACCOUNTING POLICIES
nodes.heading: NOTE 1 — ACCOUNTING POLICIES
nodes.start_phrase: The consolidated financial statements and accompanying notes are prepared in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America (“U.S. GAAP”).
nodes.summary:

- R&D expenses and software development capitalization post-technological feasibility.

- Stock-based compensation measurement and recognition; ESPP accounting.
- Income taxes: current/deferred, uncertain tax positions, valuation allowances; all deferred taxes classified as long-term.
- Fair value measurements framework (Levels 1–3), including nonrecurring impairment assessments.
- Financial instruments and investments:

  - Allowance for doubtful accounts activity disclosed.
  - Inventories at lower of cost or market; PP&E useful lives and depreciation.

- Recently adopted guidance:

  - Early adoption of balance sheet classification of deferred taxes (all noncurrent), applied retrospectively.
- Guidance not yet adopted and expected impacts:

- Exhibit 10.1 – Microsoft Corporation 2001 Stock Plan (as amended July 26, 2016):
  - Purpose: Attract/retain talent, incentivize performance, align with shareholder value.
  - Awards: Incentive Stock Options (ISOs), Nonqualified Stock Options (NQSOs), Stock Awards, and Stock Appreciation Rights (SARs).
  - Share pool and recycling: Tied to the 1991 plan’s remaining/returned shares minus 100,000,000; rules for expiration/cancellation and non-regrant of transferred options.
  - Administration: Board/Compensation Committee authority, including grant terms, FMV determination, performance goals (e.g., revenues, earnings, margins, cash flow, ROE/ROA/ROI, TSR, stock price), and ability to adjust/interpret.
  - Eligibility and limits: Employees/Consultants (ISOs only to Employees); per-participant annual caps of 20,000,000 shares for Options/SARs and 5,000,000 for Stock Awards.
  - Options: ISO/NQSO designations; $100,000 ISO rule; treatment of “Conversion Options” for acquisitions (Merger Ratio mechanics).
  - Stock Awards: Terms, vesting, forfeiture/repurchase of unvested shares upon service cessation.
  - SARs: Tandem and Stand-Alone structures; settlement in cash and/or shares; base price ≥ FMV for Stand-Alone SARs.
  - Term/vesting/repricing: Max 10-year term (5 years for 10% shareholders with ISOs); general minimum 3-year vesting with exceptions (e.g., up to 50,000,000 shares, performance-based, death/disability/retirement, Conversion Options); no repricing or cash buyouts without shareholder approval.
  - Exercise price: ISOs at ≥100% FMV (110% for 10% shareholders); NQSOs/SARs at ≥75% FMV (special FLSA rules for non-exempt at ≥85% FMV and 6-month non-exercisability); cap of 50,000,000 shares for sub-FMV NQSOs/SARs.
  - Exercise/payment/withholding: Cash/broker-assisted, share tender (for officers), and share withholding for taxes; FMV defined as Nasdaq closing price.
  - Service termination events: Post-termination exercise rules; accelerated/extended vesting and exercise windows for disability and death.
  - Transferability: Generally non-transferable except by will/descent; Board may permit limited transfers.
  - Corporate actions: Adjustments for splits/dividends/recapitalizations; treatment on dissolution, sale of assets, or mergers (assumption/substitution or temporary full exercisability).
  - Other: Amendment/termination (certain changes require shareholder approval); foreign subplans; securities law compliance; share reservation; no employment rights. Note: share counts reflect a 2-for-1 split in Feb 2003.
- Exhibit 12 – Computation of Ratios of Earnings to Fixed Charges (FY2012–FY2016):
  - Presents “Earnings” (pre-tax from continuing ops adjusted for equity method and fixed charges) and “Fixed Charges” (interest expense, capitalized debt costs, and interest component of rent).
  - Ratios: 52x (2012), 57x (2013), 43x (2014), 22x (2015), 16x (2016), with underlying totals shown.
